answer_text:
We work modulo \(99\).

The first condition says that no two distinct elements of \(A\) can be congruent modulo \(99\), because then their difference would be a multiple of \(99\).

The second condition says that no two distinct elements of \(A\) can have residues adding to \(0 \pmod{99}\), because then their sum would be a multiple of \(99\).

Now partition the residue classes modulo \(99\) into the following \(50\) groups:

\[
\{0\},\quad \{1,98\},\quad \{2,97\},\quad \ldots,\quad \{49,50\}.
\]

There are \(1\) singleton group and \(49\) two-element groups, for a total of \(50\) groups.

If \(A\) contained two numbers from the same group, then:

- In \(\{0\}\), two numbers would both be multiples of \(99\), so their difference would be a multiple of \(99\).
- In \(\{i,99-i\}\), two numbers would either have the same residue, giving a difference divisible by \(99\), or have complementary residues, giving a sum divisible by \(99\).

Thus \(A\) can contain at most one element from each of these \(50\) groups. Therefore,

\[
|A| \le 50.
\]

It remains to show that \(50\) is achievable. Take

\[
A=\{1,2,\ldots,49,99\}.
\]

All elements of \(A\) lie in \(P=\{1,2,\ldots,2014\}\). Their residues modulo \(99\) are

\[
1,2,\ldots,49,0.
\]

No two are congruent modulo \(99\), so no difference is a multiple of \(99\). Also, no two residues sum to \(0 \pmod{99}\), so no sum is a multiple of \(99\).

Hence the maximum possible number of elements in \(A\) is

\[
\boxed{50}.
\]
